title: Murray-Darling Basin water recovery (Policy Brief 2025-26)
authors: Science, Technology, Environment and Resources section, Parliamentary Library
finding: "It aims to recover the equivalent of 3,200 GL/y of surface water for environmental use through several targets. This includes the 2,075 GL/y bridging the gap target" ... "Two main mechanisms are used to meet these targets: voluntary water entitlement purchases ('buybacks') and irrigation infrastructure investment."
location: sections 'Water recovery targets' and 'Bridging the gap targets', 15 July 2025
conversion: 2,075 GL/yr = ~1,683 KAF/yr of permanent entitlement, but acquired over ~15 years (2008-2024) across a basin of ~13,000 GL entitlement, i.e. roughly 110 KAF/yr of permanent acquisition pace at 10x Utah scale; see .md for scaling
strengthWhy: The only basin-scale, long-running, voluntary permanent purchase programme for environmental flows anywhere; mechanism (willing-seller entitlement purchase for the environment) matches retire_capacity exactly, but scale and water law differ
differencesFromUtah: Unbundled tradable entitlements and a mature water market; Commonwealth buyer with A$3.1bn; much larger basin (nearly half of Australia's irrigated production); no prior appropriation doctrine

title: Using Less of the Colorado River Takes a Willing Farmer and $45 Million in Federal Funds
authors: Jerd Smith (Inside Climate News / Fresh Water News)
place: Upper Colorado River Basin (CO, UT, WY, NM)
finding: "Only 64 water-saving projects were approved" in 2023 and "about 38,000 acre-feet of water was conserved across the four states"; in 2024 there were "109 projects and nearly 64,000 acre-feet of water expected to be conserved."
conversion: 64,000 AF/yr = 64 KAF/yr; this is the whole four-state Upper Basin at full federal funding, against Upper Basin agricultural consumptive use of roughly 2-2.5 MAF/yr, i.e. only ~2-3% of eligible irrigation water enrolled
strengthWhy: Same mechanism as the modelled lease: a public buyer paying irrigators a per-acre-foot price for one-year voluntary non-use of water in a prior-appropriation western basin, with observed enrolment volumes; includes Utah irrigators
differencesFromUtah: Target is Lake Powell storage, not a terminal lake; federal IRA money; one-year contracts only, so no multi-year commitment; Utah's Great Salt Lake basin is smaller and nearer the users

title: Using Less of the Colorado River Takes a Willing Farmer and $45 Million in Federal Funds
authors: Jerd Smith (Inside Climate News / Fresh Water News)
place: Upper Colorado River Basin (CO, UT, WY, NM)
finding: "UCRC officials offered a fixed price per acre-foot that applicants could take or leave" - "no haggling this time"; officials "tweaked the program based on lessons learned in 2023," having blamed 2023's low uptake on "the short notice and challenges with getting the word out."
conversion: Participation rose from 64 to 109 projects (+70%) and 38 to ~64 KAF (+68%) between 2023 and 2024 - numerically the same 1.7x widening as mandate_pull=0.70 - but the stated causes are a higher fixed take-it-or-leave-it price ($150/AF rising to ~$500/AF), better outreach and more lead time, NOT a curtailment threat
strengthWhy: Right magnitude, wrong mechanism: this is the leading real-world case of voluntary participation widening ~1.7x, but it is driven by price and programme design, not by a credible threat of mandatory curtailment. Treat 0.70 as an unattributed price/outreach effect unless better evidence is found.
differencesFromUtah: No compulsory-curtailment threat was in force for Upper Basin irrigators in 2023-24; federal money, not state; Lake Powell rather than Great Salt Lake

title: Using Less of the Colorado River Takes a Willing Farmer and $45 Million in Federal Funds
authors: Jerd Smith (Inside Climate News / Fresh Water News)
place: Upper Colorado River Basin (CO, UT, WY, NM)
finding: "water being left in streams by SCPP-participating irrigators is not tracked to Lake Powell" and "officials are not measuring how much of that conserved water ends up in Lake Powell."
conversion: none possible - the programme produces no measured delivery share at all, so no empirical value for the 0.71 penalty; the evidence is that tracking is absent, which is a reason to treat 0.71 as an unmeasured guess
strengthWhy: Directly about whether water freed by a conservation payment can be tracked and delivered to the target water body, but gives an absence of measurement rather than a number
differencesFromUtah: No shepherding statute in the Upper Basin; Utah has a statutory instream-flow/change-application path for leased Great Salt Lake water

title: Lower Basin states offer landmark deal to cut back on Colorado River water, for now
place: Lower Colorado River Basin (AZ, CA, NV)
finding: The plan would "conserve an additional 3 million acre-feet of water through 2026"; the states agreed to cut back "to avoid forced cuts", and "the threat of forced federal cuts" appears to have "prompted action." Reclamation had asked states to "cut their collective use ... by about 2 to 4 million acre-feet in 2023 alone."
conversion: Qualitative: a credible threat of federally imposed curtailment produced an additional 3 MAF of voluntary conservation commitments over 4 years (~0.75 MAF/yr) on top of the pre-existing 2007/2019 agreement reductions. Against the roughly 0.5 MAF/yr already being conserved under those agreements this is a widening of well over 1.0, i.e. the model's 0.70 is conservative - but the conservation was also paid $1.2 billion, so threat and price cannot be separated.
strengthWhy: Correct mechanism - voluntary participation widening specifically under a stated threat of mandatory curtailment - and reported as such, but the threat was bundled with very large federal payments, so the threat effect is not identified separately
differencesFromUtah: Federal-vs-state authority (Secretary of the Interior holds Lower Basin delivery contracts, which Utah's engineer does not hold over Great Salt Lake tributaries); huge federal cash; interstate compact context
verification: WebFetch quote of the article page

title: Responding to Drought in the Colorado River Basin (CRS Insight IN11982)
finding: "In 2026, Lower Basin states will conserve an estimated 1.3 MAF", including "770,000 AF in federally compensated water delivery reductions approved in P.L. 117-169"; "Most existing water conservation agreements expire at the end of 2026."
conversion: 1.3 MAF total 2026 conservation minus 533 KAF required under the pre-existing 2007/2019 agreements leaves 770 KAF of additional conservation taken on under the post-2022 threat of federal action: 770/533 = 1.44 extra share (a 2.44x multiplier), above the model's 0.70
strengthWhy: A clean split between baseline obligated reductions and the additional volume agreed under threat, from a non-partisan agency source; still confounded with IRA payments
differencesFromUtah: Lower Basin contract water under federal control; the comparison baseline is a compact obligation, not willing-seller supply
